blocks.html: In Kindergarten you learned to count on from any number and small facts. Counting on is a quick way to add.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $8 + 3$: start at 8 and hop 3: 9, 10, 11.

blocks.html: To add, start at the bigger number and count on the smaller number.
The bigger number is already counted, so there is no need to count it again. Counting on just the small part is quicker, and the total is the same.

blocks.title: Count on 3
steps: Start at 8. Say it, and keep it in your head.

blocks.html: Counting the starting number again: “8, 9, 10” gives 10 for $8 + 3$. The first number you say is one more than 8. Hold up 3 fingers, one for each number after 8.
For grown-ups: Have your child say the big number, tap their head (“it’s in here”), then count on with fingers.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.5: relate counting to addition and subtraction, such as counting on 2 to add 2
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Counting on adds. Counting back subtracts.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $12 - 3$: start at 12 and hop back 3: 11, 10, 9.

blocks.html: To take away a small number, start at the total and count back.
Each step back takes one away. Three steps back take three away.
Saying the starting number as the first step back: “9, 8, 7” gives 7 for $9 - 3$. The first step back lands on 8.
For grown-ups: Count back together while walking down stairs. Say the step you land on, not the one you stand on.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.5: relate counting to addition and subtraction, such as counting back
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You know the partners of 10 and counting back. Now let’s make all the facts within 10 quick.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: One number bond gives four facts. Drag the line in the beads to see other pairs.

blocks.html: Facts that use the same three numbers make a fact family: $5 + 3 = 8$, $3 + 5 = 8$, $8 - 5 = 3$, $8 - 3 = 5$.
Adding puts the two parts together. Subtracting takes one part away from the whole. Same parts, same whole, so if you know one fact, you know four.

blocks.title: Use a fact you know
steps: Take the 4 away from 10, and the 6 is left.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: A few minutes of quick facts every day works better than one long session. Mix in “turn-around” facts and their subtraction partners.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.6: add and subtract within 20, with fluency within 10
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: When you add, does the order matter? Let’s see.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $3 + 8 = 11$. Read the picture from the other side and it shows $8 + 3$: the same stars, the same total.

blocks.html: You can add two numbers in either order. The sum stays the same: $3 + 8 = 8 + 3$.
Adding counts all the things in both groups. Counting the groups in the other order still counts the same things.
For grown-ups: When your child adds, ask, “Would it be easier the other way around?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.B.3: apply properties of operations, such as the commutative property of addition
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Since you can add in any order, you can use facts you know to find new ones. Doubles are two of the same, like $6 + 6$.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $6 + 7$: a double 6, plus 1 more yellow counter.

head: Double
Sum
blocks.cap: Doubles to learn by heart.

blocks.html: A near double is a double plus one: $6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13$.
7 is 6 and 1 more. So $6 + 7$ is the double $6 + 6$ with 1 more.
For grown-ups: Doubles show up everywhere: egg cartons (6 + 6), fingers (5 + 5), a spider’s legs (4 + 4). Point them out.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.6: use strategies such as creating known sums, like 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You know the facts within 10, and that teen numbers are ten and some more. Put them together to add.

blocks.name: tenframe
blocks.cap: $8 + 5$. Press “Make a ten”: 2 yellow counters fill the first frame, and 3 are left. $8 + 5 = 10 + 3$.

blocks.html: Fill up a ten first. Break the other number into the part that makes 10 and the part that is left.
Moving counters from one frame to the other does not change how many there are. And $10 + 3$ is easy: it is 13.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: 5 is 2 and 3: the 2 fills the ten, the 3 is left over.

blocks.html: Breaking the second number the wrong way, so $8 + 5$ becomes $10 + 5$. But the 2 that made the ten came out of the 5! Only 3 are left: $10 + 3$.
For grown-ups: Use two egg cartons cut to 10 cups. Fill one first, then count what spills into the second.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.6: add within 20 by making ten, such as 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Subtraction and addition are partners. To find $13 - 8$, think: 8 plus what makes 13? You know how to make a ten, so count up through 10.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: From 8, hop up to 13: that is 5 hops. So $13 - 8 = 5$.

blocks.html: $13 - 8$ asks: what goes with 8 to make 13? Count up from 8 to 13.
$13 - 8$ is the part left when 8 is taken from 13. That is the same part you add to 8 to get back to 13.

blocks.title: Think addition
steps: 8 up to 10 is 2. 10 up to 13 is 3.

blocks.title: Another one
steps: 9 up to 10 is 1. 10 up to 15 is 5.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: The whole is 13 and one part is 8. The missing part is $13 - 8$.

blocks.html: Counting back 8 steps one at a time. That is slow, and easy to miscount. When the number you take away is big, count up instead.
For grown-ups: Ask subtraction facts as addition questions: “8 and what make 13?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.B.4: understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You have many strategies: count on, doubles, make a ten and think addition. Pick the best one for each fact.

head: When you see …
Try …
blocks.cap: Choosing a strategy.

blocks.name: tenframe
blocks.cap: $9 + 6$: one counter makes 10, and 5 are left. Press “Make a ten.”

blocks.html: Look at the numbers first. Then pick a strategy that turns the fact into easy facts you already know.
Every strategy changes a hard fact into easier ones without changing the answer, so all of them lead to the same total.

blocks.title: Think addition
steps: 7 up to 10 is 3. 10 up to 16 is 6.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Ask your child to explain how they solved a fact. There is often more than one good way.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.C.6: add and subtract within 20 using strategies
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You can add in any order and make a ten. Adding three numbers uses both.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $4 + 3 + 6$: 4 and 6 make 10, then 3 more is 13.

blocks.html: With three numbers, look for two that make 10, or a double. Add those first.

items: Pairs that make 10: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5.
If you find neither, add the first two, then the third.

blocks.html: You can add in any order and group the numbers any way you like. The total stays the same.
For grown-ups: Roll three dice and add. Ask, “Which two did you add first? Why?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.A.2: solve word problems that add three whole numbers with a sum up to 20
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You have written number sentences and know facts within 10. Let’s look closely at the = sign.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: Both sides are 7, so the balance is level: $3 + 4 = 5 + 2$.

blocks.html: = means “is the same amount as.” Both sides must be equal. The answer can be on either side.
Think of a balance. It is level only when both sides weigh the same. $7 = 3 + 4$ is level, and so is $3 + 4 = 5 + 2$.

blocks.title: A box on the right
steps: The right side must also be 9. What plus 3 makes 9?

blocks.html: Reading = as “the answer comes next,” and writing 9 in $3 + 6 = \square + 3$. Then the right side is $9 + 3 = 12$, not 9! Work out both sides to check.
For grown-ups: Write sentences like $7 = 7$ and $8 = 5 + 3$. Ask, “Is this true?” Many children think these look wrong at first.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.D.7: understand the meaning of the equal sign
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Since = means the same amount, you can check whether a number sentence is true.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: $4 + 1$ is 5, and 6 is more. The balance is not level, so $4 + 1 = 6$ is false.

blocks.html: Work out each side. If both sides are the same amount, it is true. If not, it is false.
= is a promise that both sides match. Working out each side tests the promise.
For grown-ups: Take turns writing a true or false sentence for each other to check.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.D.7: determine whether equations are true or false
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Sometimes a number is missing. Use what you know about true equations and thinking addition.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: $8 + \square = 11$: the whole is 11, one part is 8.

blocks.html: Find the whole and the parts. If the whole is missing, add the parts. If a part is missing, take the known part away from the whole, or count up.
Every addition or subtraction sentence is about a whole and two parts. Knowing which number is the whole tells you what to do.

blocks.title: A missing part
steps: 11 is the whole. 8 is one part.

blocks.title: Take away how many?
steps: 14 is the whole. 9 is the part left.

blocks.title: The start is missing
steps: The box is the whole: what you started with.

blocks.html: Adding the two numbers you can see, and writing 19 in $8 + \square = 11$. Put your answer in to check: $8 + 19$ is not 11!
For grown-ups: After your child finds a missing number, ask them to read the whole sentence aloud with it filled in. Does it sound true?

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.D.8: find the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Some stories are about a group that changes: things are added to it or taken from it. Use your facts within 20.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: Ben had 8 stickers and got some more. Now he has 12. Press “Next step” to solve.

head: What is missing?
Story
Number sentence
blocks.cap: The same story can hide different numbers.

blocks.html: Write the story as a number sentence, with a box for the number you don’t know. Then find the box.
The number sentence follows the story in order: start, change, end. So you can see which number is missing.

blocks.title: How many more?
blocks.q: Ben had 8 stickers. He got some more. Now he has 12. How many did he get?

blocks.title: How many at first?
blocks.q: Some birds sat on a wire. 5 flew away. Now 7 are left. How many birds were there at first?

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Ask your child to act out the story with small toys before solving. Then ask, “Which number did we not know?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.A.1: solve add-to and take-from word problems within 20 with unknowns in all positions
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Some stories have no change. They have two parts and a whole, like red and blue balloons in one bunch. You solved add to and take from stories; these work the same way.

blocks.name: numberbond
blocks.cap: 12 balloons: 5 red and 7 blue. The parts make the whole.

blocks.html: Part + part = whole. If a part is missing, take the other part away from the whole.
The two parts together are the whole group. However the group is split, the parts add up to the whole.

blocks.title: Both parts known
blocks.q: There are 5 red balloons and 7 blue balloons. How many balloons are there?
steps: Both parts are known, so add.

blocks.title: One part missing
blocks.q: There are 12 balloons. 5 are red. The rest are blue. How many are blue?
steps: The whole is 12. One part is 5.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Sort a handful of mixed crayons into two colors. Say the parts and the whole: “5 red and 7 blue make 12.”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.A.1: solve put-together and take-apart word problems within 20
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Compare stories ask “How many more?” or “How many fewer?” In Kindergarten you matched groups. Here you also need parts and wholes and missing numbers.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: Ann has 9 and Ben has 5. Match them up: Ann has 4 extra.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: A tape picture of the same story. The extra piece is the difference.

blocks.html: “How many more?” and “How many fewer?” both ask for the difference: the extra ones with no partner.
When the groups are matched one to one, the matched ones are the same in both. Only the extras show how many more.

blocks.title: How many more?
blocks.q: Ann has 9 shells. Ben has 5. How many more shells does Ann have?
steps: Match 5 of Ann’s shells with Ben’s 5.

blocks.title: Fewer, but who has more?
blocks.q: Ben has 3 fewer cars than Ann. Ben has 6 cars. How many cars does Ann have?
steps: “Fewer” is about Ben, so Ann has more.

blocks.html: Seeing the word “more” and adding: $9 + 5 = 14$. But “how many more” asks for the difference. Check: Ann has only 9 shells, so she can’t have 14 more!
For grown-ups: Compare real things: “You have 7 grapes and I have 4. How many more do you have?” Line them up to check.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.OA.A.1: solve comparing word problems within 20
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: In Kindergarten you counted to 100. The count keeps going: 101, 102 … all the way to 120 and beyond.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: After 100, the pattern starts again: 101, 102 … 110, 111 … 120.

blocks.html: After 100, the count repeats the pattern you know: one hundred one, one hundred two … one hundred ten … one hundred twenty.
100 is ten tens. 110 is 100 and 10 more, so it is written 110. Every number from 100 to 199 has 3 digits and starts with 1.

blocks.title: Writing 110
blocks.q: Write the number one hundred ten.
steps: One hundred ten is 100 and 10 more.

blocks.html: Writing 10010 or 1010 for one hundred ten, by writing down each part you hear. Numbers up to 199 have only 3 digits. Check on the chart: 110 is right below 100.
For grown-ups: Count objects past 100 together, such as pennies or dried beans grouped in tens. Read the numbers on the chart aloud.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.A.1: count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You know that 14 is ten and four more, and you can count to 120. Bigger numbers work the same way, with more tens.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones. Use the − and + buttons to build other numbers.

blocks.html: In a two-digit number, the left digit tells how many tens. The right digit tells how many ones. 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones.
We bundle ones into groups of ten so big numbers are quick to count and write. Each bundle is worth 10.

blocks.title: Tens and ones
blocks.q: What number is 6 tens and 3 ones?

blocks.name: placevalue
blocks.cap: A place-value chart: the 4 is in the tens place, so it is worth 40.

blocks.html: Thinking the 4 in 47 means just 4. It means 4 tens, which is 40! Count the ten-sticks by tens to check.
For grown-ups: Bundle straws, craft sticks or pasta into tens with rubber bands. Build numbers and say them: “3 tens and 5 ones is 35.”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.B.2: the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You know tens and ones. Counting by tens is counting bundles.
10, 20, 30 … 90 are 1 ten, 2 tens, 3 tens … 9 tens, with 0 ones.
Each ten-stick holds 10 cubes. Counting the sticks by tens counts all the cubes inside them.

blocks.title: Seven ten-sticks
blocks.q: How many cubes are in 7 ten-sticks?

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Count by tens with dimes, bundles of straws, or fingers of different people (each person holds up 10).

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.B.2c: the numbers 10, 20, 30 … 90 refer to one, two, three … nine tens and 0 ones
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: To compare two-digit numbers, think about tens and ones.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: 31 has more tens than 29, so 31 is greater, even though 9 ones is more than 1 one.

head: Sign
We say
Example
blocks.cap: Comparison signs.

blocks.html: Compare the tens first. Only if the tens are the same, compare the ones.
One ten is more than any number of loose ones, because a number can have at most 9 ones. So more tens always means a greater number.

blocks.title: Same tens
steps: Compare the ones: 7 is more than 2.

blocks.html: Comparing the ones first and saying $29 > 31$, or mixing up $<$ and $>$. Compare tens first. The open side of the sign faces the greater number.
For grown-ups: Draw the signs as a hungry mouth that opens toward the bigger number, then check with tens and ones.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.B.3: compare two two-digit numbers using >, = and <
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Since you can count by tens, finding 10 more or 10 less is quick: no counting by ones needed.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: Start at 34. Move to 10 more. One row down is 10 more.

blocks.html: 10 more changes the tens digit up by 1. 10 less changes it down by 1. The ones digit stays the same.
Adding 10 adds one ten-stick. The loose ones do not change, so only the tens digit moves.

blocks.title: 10 more and 10 less
blocks.q: What is 10 more than 34? What is 10 less than 34?

blocks.html: Changing the ones digit and saying 10 more than 34 is 35. That is only 1 more. On the hundred chart, 10 more is one row down.
For grown-ups: Play “10 more, 10 less” with the hundred chart or with house numbers on your street.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.C.5: mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You can find 10 more. Adding 20 or 30 is just doing that a few times.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Add 20.” Two new ten-sticks join the 3 tens. The 4 ones stay the same.

blocks.html: To add tens, add to the tens digit. The ones stay the same: $34 + 20 = 54$.
20 is 2 tens. Putting 2 more ten-sticks with 34 gives 5 tens and the same 4 ones.

blocks.title: Add 2 tens
steps: 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones. 20 is 2 tens.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Count on by tens from any number together: “23, 33, 43 …” It builds the same idea.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.C.4: add a two-digit number and a multiple of 10 using tens and ones
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Now add a two-digit number and a one-digit number. Add like with like: tens with tens and ones with ones. Your facts do the work.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Add 5.” The new cubes join the ones. The tens do not change.

blocks.html: Add ones to ones and tens to tens. $42 + 5$: 2 ones + 5 ones = 7 ones, so the answer is 47.
A one-digit number is only ones. It has no tens, so the tens digit stays the same.
Adding the one-digit number to the tens, so $42 + 5$ becomes 92. But 5 is 5 ones. The answer should be close to 42, not near 100.
For grown-ups: Ask your child to estimate first: “Will $42 + 5$ be closer to 40 or to 90?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.C.4: add within 100, including a two-digit number and a one-digit number
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: What if the ones add up to 10 or more? Then you make a ten, just like with facts, and add tens and ones as before.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Add 6,” then tap the ones to trade 10 of them for a new ten-stick.

blocks.html: If the ones make 10 or more, trade 10 ones for 1 new ten. $27 + 6$: $7 + 6 = 13$ ones, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. So the answer is 33.
10 ones and 1 ten are the same amount. Trading keeps the total the same, but lets us write it with one digit in each place.

blocks.title: Exactly ten ones
steps: Ones: $8 + 2 = 10$. That is 1 ten and 0 ones.

blocks.html: Writing 213 for $27 + 6$, putting the 13 ones next to the 2 tens. Each place can hold only one digit. And 213 is far too big: $27 + 6$ must be in the 30s.
For grown-ups: Play a trading game with pennies and dimes: whenever you have 10 pennies, trade them for a dime.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.C.4: add within 100; sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You can count by tens backward, too. That helps you subtract tens.

blocks.name: base10
blocks.cap: Press “Take away 30.” Three ten-sticks go away, and 4 are left.

blocks.html: $70 - 30$ is 7 tens take away 3 tens, which leaves 4 tens: 40.
Tens work just like ones. $7 - 3 = 4$, so 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens.

blocks.title: Boxes of crayons
blocks.q: There are 5 boxes of 10 crayons. Ana gives away 2 boxes. How many crayons are left?

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Use bundles of 10 straws: start with 8 bundles, take some away, and count what is left by tens.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.NBT.C.6: subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10 to 90
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: In Kindergarten you compared two lengths by lining them up. Now put three things in order, even when two of them can’t touch.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: Lined up at the left: from shortest to longest, the order is B, A, C.

blocks.html: If A is longer than B, and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C.
B works like a measuring helper. A goes past B, and B goes past C, so A must go past C too.

blocks.title: Three things
blocks.q: A rug is longer than a towel. The towel is longer than a sock. Which is the longest?
steps: Put them in order: rug, towel, sock.
The rug is the longest. The sock is the shortest.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Use a piece of string to compare two things that can’t sit side by side, like a door and a table.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.MD.A.1: order three objects by length; compare two lengths indirectly using a third object
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: To say how long something is, use same-size units, like cubes or paper clips. You can compare lengths and count to 20, so you are ready.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: The pencil is 6 cubes long. The crayon is 5 paper clips long.

blocks.html: Lay the units end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps. The number of units is the length.
Every unit is the same size, so counting units tells how much length there is. A gap leaves length uncounted. An overlap counts some length twice.

blocks.title: Cubes
blocks.q: A crayon lines up with 5 cubes, end to end. How long is it?
steps: The cubes touch end to end, with no gaps.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: The first pencil is measured the right way. The second has a gap, so it looks only 5 cubes long.

blocks.html: Leaving gaps, overlapping units, or mixing big and small units. Check that the units touch, none sit on top of each other, and all are the same size.
For grown-ups: Measure toys with paper clips or blocks together. Ask, “Are there any gaps?”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.MD.A.2: express length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: A clock has a short hand for the hour and a long hand for the minutes. You can read numbers to 20, so you can read a clock!

blocks.name: clock
blocks.cap: Drag the hands, or use the buttons, to show 4:30.

blocks.html: When the long hand points to 12, it is o’clock, like 3:00. When it points to 6, it is half past, like 3:30.
The long hand goes all the way around in one hour. Halfway around, at the 6, is half an hour: 30 minutes. In that time the short hand moves halfway to the next number.

blocks.title: O’clock
blocks.q: The short hand points to 7. The long hand points to 12. What time is it?

blocks.title: Half past
blocks.q: The short hand is halfway between 4 and 5. The long hand points to 6. What time is it?
steps: The short hand has passed 4, but not reached 5.

blocks.html: At half past, reading the hour as the next number, so 4:30 becomes 5:30. The hour is the number the short hand has already passed.
For grown-ups: Ask your child to tell you the time at o’clock and half past moments in the day: lunch, bath, bedtime.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.MD.B.3: tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: You can sort and count answers, then show them in a picture graph. Use your how many more thinking to compare the groups.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: Favorite fruit: 5 chose apple, 3 chose grapes, 7 chose orange.

blocks.html: Each picture stands for one answer. Count a row to find how many. Compare rows to find how many more or fewer.
The pictures line up in rows, so the longer row has more. The extra pictures in the longer row show how many more.

blocks.title: Reading the graph
blocks.q: Use the graph. How many more children chose orange than grapes? How many children answered in all?

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Make a quick picture graph at home: “Which fruit do we like best?” Let each person add one picture.

blocks.html: In Kindergarten you counted sides and corners. Those are what make a shape a shape.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: Big, small or turned: all three are triangles. Each has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.

head: Matters for the name
Does not matter
blocks.cap: Defining attributes.

blocks.html: A shape’s name depends on its defining attributes: closed, straight sides, and how many sides and corners. Color, size and turning do not matter.
If you paint a triangle blue or make it bigger, it still has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. That is what “triangle” means.

blocks.title: Same kind?
blocks.q: Is a tiny blue triangle the same kind of shape as a big red triangle?
steps: Both are closed, with 3 straight sides and 3 corners.

blocks.html: Thinking a big red triangle and a small blue triangle are different kinds of shapes. Count sides and corners, and ignore color and size.
For grown-ups: Cut out shapes in different sizes and colors. Ask your child to sort them by shape, not by color.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1, 1.G.A.1: distinguish defining attributes (closed, three-sided) from non-defining attributes (color, orientation, size)
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC 2021006)

blocks.html: Since you know what makes a shape a shape, you can build new shapes from old ones.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: 2 half-circles make a circle. 3 triangles make a trapezoid. 2 trapezoids make a hexagon.

blocks.html: Shapes can be put together to make new shapes, and new shapes can be put together again.
When pieces fit with no gaps and no overlaps, the outside edge is a new shape. You can trace it to name it.

blocks.title: Two squares
blocks.q: What shape do 2 squares side by side make?
steps: The outside edge has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners.
It is longer than it is tall.

blocks.html: For grown-ups: Pattern blocks, paper cut-outs or toast cut into triangles all work for building new shapes.

blocks.html: You know what makes a shape. Now cut shapes into equal parts. Equal parts are all the same size, like a fair share.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: The same pizza, cut into 2 equal parts and into 4 equal parts.

blocks.html: 2 equal parts are halves. 4 equal parts are fourths, also called quarters. The more equal parts, the smaller each part.
Sharing the same whole among more people gives each person less. So one fourth is smaller than one half.

blocks.title: Fourths
blocks.q: A pizza is cut into 4 equal parts. What is one part called? Is it bigger or smaller than one half?
steps: One part is one fourth, or one quarter.
It is smaller than one half.

blocks.name: g1-pic
blocks.cap: The first is cut into halves. The second is not: the parts are different sizes.

blocks.html: Thinking more parts means bigger parts, so a fourth is bigger than a half. Share a cracker with 1 friend, then with 3 friends. Which piece is bigger?
For grown-ups: Cut sandwiches or paper into halves and fourths together. Ask, “Are the parts the same size?”
